title: Peripheral Arterial, Venous & Aortic Disorders: Limb Perfusion, Thromboembolism and Vascular Rescue
html:
Peripheral vascular disorders can threaten a limb, the lungs, the brain, or the entire circulation. The RN distinguishes reduced arterial inflow from impaired venous return, identifies acute change against chronic disease, and acts quickly when tissue viability or cardiopulmonary stability is at risk. A pulse finding, swollen leg, or pain score is only one cue; pattern, symmetry, onset, and perfusion determine urgency.

Learning goals

  • Differentiate peripheral artery disease, acute limb ischemia, chronic venous insufficiency, DVT, PE, and aortic emergencies.
  • Perform and document a focused bilateral neurovascular assessment.
  • Prioritize immediate actions for an acutely threatened limb, massive PE, aneurysm rupture, or aortic dissection.
  • Apply medication, compression, wound, mobility, and post-revascularization safeguards.
  • Recognize bleeding, reperfusion injury, compartment syndrome, and graft or access complications.
  • Teach risk reduction, foot protection, anticoagulation safety, and emergency symptoms.

Arteries deliver; veins return

Arterial disease reduces oxygenated blood reaching tissues. Chronic atherosclerotic narrowing causes peripheral artery disease (PAD), while embolus, thrombosis, graft occlusion, dissection, or trauma can abruptly stop flow. Venous disease impairs return to the heart. Valve failure produces venous hypertension and edema; thrombus can obstruct a deep vein and embolize to the lungs.

Do not use the vague label “poor circulation” as a diagnosis. Determine whether the pattern suggests arterial inflow failure, venous congestion, lymphatic dysfunction, systemic fluid overload, infection, neuropathy, or overlapping disease.

Build a bilateral neurovascular baseline

Ask about onset, location, quality, exertional pattern, rest pain, swelling, heaviness, wounds, color or temperature change, numbness, weakness, prior thrombosis, vascular procedures, immobility, cancer, pregnancy or postpartum status, hormones, smoking, diabetes, kidney disease, and current antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy.

Compare both limbs for color, temperature, capillary refill, pulses, edema, skin integrity, hair and nail changes, movement, sensation, pain, and circumference at a reproducible landmark when indicated. Use Doppler assessment when trained and a pulse is difficult to palpate. Document the signal and location rather than writing “Doppler pulse.” Marking an assessed pulse site can support serial comparison after a procedure.

Trend the whole limb
A palpable pulse does not exclude serious ischemia, and edema does not prove DVT. Compare pain, color, warmth, refill, motor and sensory function, pulse quality, and change over time.

PAD may be symptomatic or silent

Classic claudication is reproducible muscle discomfort with walking that improves after rest. PAD can also present as slower walking, fatigue, weakness, atypical leg symptoms, or no reported symptoms. Advanced chronic limb-threatening ischemia may produce ischemic rest pain, nonhealing ulcer, or gangrene.

Arterial skin findings can include coolness, pallor with elevation, dependent rubor, delayed refill, reduced hair, thick nails, weak pulses, and distal ulcers with a pale or necrotic base. Neuropathy and diabetes may reduce pain despite severe ischemia. Do not apply heating pads to an insensate or poorly perfused limb; burns and increased metabolic demand can worsen injury.

ABI supports diagnosis but has limits

The ankle-brachial index compares ankle and arm systolic pressures. A reduced ratio supports PAD, while noncompressible calcified arteries—common with diabetes or kidney disease—can produce a falsely high value. Toe pressures, waveforms, exercise testing, duplex ultrasound, CT angiography, MR angiography, or invasive angiography may be needed according to the clinical question.

Measure with the validated method and correct cuffs. Do not delay emergency vascular evaluation for an ABI when acute limb ischemia is suspected.

Acute limb ischemia is a limb emergency

Sudden pain, pallor, pulselessness, coolness, paresthesia, and paralysis are classic warning cues. Sensory loss or motor weakness signals advanced threat. The limb may not display all findings, and a Doppler signal can disappear before a pulse becomes visibly different.

Notify the vascular or emergency team immediately, keep the limb at rest in a neutral or dependent position unless directed otherwise, protect it from pressure and temperature extremes, maintain NPO status in anticipation of intervention, obtain IV access and ordered studies, and prepare anticoagulation or revascularization under protocol. Do not elevate a severely ischemic limb, massage it, apply compression, or delay for routine care.

Chronic PAD treatment protects limb and life

PAD is systemic atherosclerotic disease and raises myocardial infarction, stroke, amputation, and mortality risk. Management commonly includes tobacco cessation, antiplatelet and lipid-lowering therapy, blood-pressure and diabetes management, structured exercise, foot care, and revascularization for selected symptoms or limb threat. Medication selection must reflect bleeding risk and other vascular disease.

Structured walking can improve function in stable chronic PAD, but new rest pain, tissue loss, infection, or acute change requires evaluation before exercise. Inspect feet daily, wash and dry gently, moisturize intact skin but not between toes, wear protective well-fitting shoes, avoid self-treatment of corns or nails when high risk, and report blisters, discoloration, drainage, or wounds promptly.

Venous insufficiency produces pressure and inflammation

Chronic venous hypertension often causes dependent edema, aching or heaviness that worsens with standing, brown hemosiderin staining, stasis dermatitis, and shallow irregular ulcers near the medial ankle. Elevation, walking and calf-muscle activation, skin care, wound care, and correctly fitted compression may improve return.

Compression is not automatically safe. Confirm arterial adequacy and the prescribed level before applying it, particularly when pulses are weak, the foot is cool, or mixed disease is suspected. Avoid wrinkles, constricting bands, and pressure over fragile skin. Reassess color, warmth, sensation, pain, and distal perfusion.

DVT: suspect from risk and pattern, confirm with testing

Venous thromboembolism includes deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism. DVT may cause unilateral swelling, tenderness, warmth, or discoloration, but many clients have few or no symptoms. Risk reflects venous stasis, endothelial injury, and hypercoagulability: surgery, trauma, immobility, cancer, prior VTE, pregnancy or postpartum state, estrogen exposure, inherited or acquired thrombophilia, serious illness, and central venous devices can contribute.

Do not massage a suspected DVT and do not use Homan sign; it is unreliable and can cause harm. Protect the client from falls, obtain the history and bilateral measurements, notify the team, and prepare risk-guided D-dimer and compression ultrasound or other imaging. A positive D-dimer is nonspecific, while a negative result is useful only within an appropriate probability pathway.

PE can occur without obvious leg symptoms

Sudden unexplained dyspnea, pleuritic chest discomfort, tachypnea, tachycardia, hypoxemia, hemoptysis, anxiety, lightheadedness, syncope, or hypotension may indicate pulmonary embolism. A client can have PE without visible DVT. Massive or high-risk PE can cause obstructive shock, acute right-ventricular failure, cyanosis, altered mentation, and cardiac arrest.

Activate emergency support, assess ABCs and perfusion, apply oxygen for hypoxemia, place the client on cardiac and oxygen monitoring, establish IV access, limit exertion, and prepare diagnostic imaging and anticoagulation when authorized. Hemodynamic instability may require thrombolysis, catheter-based therapy, surgical embolectomy, or advanced support after rapid contraindication assessment.

Anticoagulation prevents extension but creates bleeding risk

Before therapy, review active bleeding, prior intracranial hemorrhage, recent surgery or trauma, pregnancy, weight, kidney and liver function, hemoglobin, platelets, interacting drugs, and last anticoagulant dose. Unfractionated heparin, low-molecular-weight heparin, direct oral anticoagulants, and warfarin have different monitoring, reversal, renal, procedural, and pregnancy considerations.

Assess bruising, gums, urine, stool, emesis, menstrual or postpartum bleeding, access sites, abdominal or back pain, headache, neurologic change, pressure, pulse, and hemoglobin trend. A falling platelet count with new thrombosis during heparin exposure raises concern for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia and requires immediate protocol-directed action; do not simply switch to another heparin product.

VTE prevention is a reliability process

Assess risk and bleeding contraindications on admission and when the condition changes. Use prescribed pharmacologic prophylaxis, intermittent pneumatic compression, early safe mobility, hydration appropriate to the client, and line care. Ensure mechanical devices are correctly fitted and actually operating; remove and replace them for skin care and ambulation as directed.

Immobility orders, missed prophylaxis, procedures, and transitions create gaps. Clarify when anticoagulants should stop and restart and document the plan. Compression devices are not placed over a known acute DVT unless specifically directed.

Aortic aneurysm may be silent until catastrophe

An aortic aneurysm is a weakened, enlarged segment that can rupture or dissect. Risk varies with location, size, growth, family or genetic conditions, smoking, hypertension, atherosclerosis, and other factors. Stable aneurysms require surveillance and risk-factor management; the absence of pain does not guarantee low risk.

Sudden severe chest, back, abdominal, shoulder, neck, or jaw pain; syncope; shock; a new pulsatile abdominal finding; neurologic deficit; limb ischemia; or rapidly falling pressure may signal rupture or dissection. Call emergency support, maintain bed rest, establish large-bore access as directed, prepare blood and imaging, and monitor perfusion. Do not repeatedly or deeply palpate a suspected abdominal aneurysm.

Aortic dissection threatens every branch vessel

A dissection begins when blood enters the aortic wall and separates its layers. It can impair flow to the coronary, carotid, spinal, renal, mesenteric, or limb arteries and may cause tamponade or aortic regurgitation. Pulse or pressure asymmetry, focal neurologic change, acute kidney injury, abdominal pain, or limb ischemia can accompany abrupt severe pain.

Urgent therapy reduces aortic-wall shear through protocol-directed heart-rate control followed by pressure management as needed, while surgery or endovascular repair is arranged according to anatomy. Analgesia, continuous monitoring, frequent neurologic and peripheral perfusion checks, and rapid escalation of change are essential.

After revascularization, reperfusion can also injure

After angioplasty, stenting, thrombectomy, bypass, or aneurysm repair, compare the limb with its preprocedure baseline. Monitor access or incision, bleeding, hematoma, pulses or Doppler signals, color, temperature, refill, pain, movement, sensation, urine output, kidney function, hemoglobin, and hemodynamics. Sudden loss of a pulse or return of ischemic pain can indicate reocclusion or graft compromise.

Reperfused muscle can swell and release potassium, acid, and myoglobin. Escalating pain out of proportion, pain with passive stretch, tense swelling, paresthesia, weakness, or declining perfusion suggests compartment syndrome. A pulse may remain present. Notify the surgical team immediately; do not wait for pulselessness.

Wounds reveal the circulation beneath them

Describe location, dimensions, depth, tissue, drainage, odor after cleansing, surrounding skin, pain, and infection cues. Arterial ulcers are often distal with sharply defined edges and poor perfusion; venous ulcers are commonly shallow and irregular in the gaiter area with edema. Diabetes, neuropathy, pressure, infection, and mixed arterial-venous disease can alter appearance.

Do not debride stable dry ischemic eschar or apply compression without an authorized vascular and wound plan. Infection plus ischemia is especially dangerous because antibiotic delivery and healing are impaired. Fever may be absent in older or immunocompromised clients.

Apply clinical judgment

  1. Recognize cues: Determine onset, pain pattern, limb symmetry, color, temperature, pulses, Doppler signals, refill, edema, motor and sensory function, wounds, breathing, pressure, VTE risks, medications, and procedures.
  2. Analyze cues: Distinguish arterial inflow failure from venous congestion, chronic baseline from acute change, DVT from alternative swelling, and local limb disease from systemic instability.
  3. Prioritize hypotheses: Acute limb ischemia, massive PE, ruptured aneurysm, aortic dissection, major bleeding, graft occlusion, and compartment syndrome require immediate action.
  4. Generate solutions: Protect perfusion, activate vascular or emergency resources, obtain targeted imaging, prepare anticoagulation or reperfusion, and prevent pressure, bleeding, and embolic harm.
  5. Take action: Keep a threatened limb safe, support ABCs for PE or shock, administer ordered therapy with monitoring, and perform frequent comparable neurovascular checks.
  6. Evaluate outcomes: Reassess pain, pulses, Doppler signals, color, temperature, refill, movement, sensation, swelling, breathing, hemodynamics, bleeding, labs, wounds, and teach-back.

Clinical example

A client who had femoral embolectomy develops rapidly increasing calf pain despite analgesia. The foot remains warm with a Doppler pulse, but passive toe movement causes severe pain and the calf is tense. The RN recognizes that a present pulse does not exclude compartment syndrome, keeps the limb in the ordered position, stops delays for routine care, immediately notifies the vascular team, and prepares for urgent pressure evaluation and possible fasciotomy while continuing motor, sensory, perfusion, renal, potassium, and rhythm monitoring.

Vascular diagnosis, ABI interpretation, compression, anticoagulation, thrombolysis, revascularization, aortic management, wound care, and emergency treatment require current clinical data, authorized orders, local protocols, specialist input, and qualified supervision. This lesson is not medical advice, clinical decision support, continuing education, or an official ACC, AHA, CDC, or NCSBN product.
